description: "The 2015 MacBook Pro is a temporary host for IDAHO-VAULT, not its permanent storage medium"
metadata:
  type: project
---

Logan's MacBookPro12,1 (Early 2015, Broadwell i7-5557U, 16 GB, 1 TB SSD) is an
aged desk machine left running at home — **not** the vault's permanent physical
medium (stated 2026-08-20). macOS 12.7.6 is the terminal OS for this hardware
(Ventura dropped 2015 MBPs), so it is permanently off Apple's patch track and
Homebrew classes it Tier 3.

**Why it matters:** Do not optimize storage decisions around fitting the vault on
this disk. The vault is 475 GB (205 GB of it `.git`, 145 GB of that LFS) against a
1 TB volume that hit 100% on 2026-08-19. Disk pressure here is a transitional
constraint, not a reason to destroy data — in particular not a reason to
`git gc --prune=now` (which would delete 94 recoverable dangling commits including
the Aug 12 reunification merge `440dfbebf`) or `git lfs prune` (145 GB that may
exist nowhere else).

**How to apply:** Frame `.git` size questions as "what migrates" rather than "what
fits." Prefer archiving to external media over deletion — `/Volumes/Time_Machine`
(1.8 TB, ~1.1 TB free) and `/Volumes/My_Passport` are attached. Work product is on
ZBFURY, the employer-supplied machine. See [[idaho-vault-storage-architecture]].

**Migration rationale (2026-08-20):** Time Machine was moved to the 2 TB LaCie
Rugged because the 1 TB My_Passport could not hold more than a single full laptop
backup. Migrating the vault off the internal drive fixes both ends — the laptop's
867 GB drops by ~475 GB, and the shrunken backup set fits comfortably again.
Sequence matters: migrate and verify FIRST, then exclude the vault from Time
Machine. TM is currently the only thing backing up a vault with no verified clean
copy elsewhere. Logan has multiple drives; destination is his call.

It's failing hardware — the CPU, specifically. Not software, not something a reinstall fixes.

## What the logs say

Six kernel panics since Aug 31, and all six are the same **uncorrectable machine check exception**:

```
IA32_MC1_STATUS: 0xbf80000000000114
```

Decoded: VAL, UC (uncorrected), EN, MISCV, ADDRV, **PCC** (processor context corrupt), error code `0x0114` = cache-hierarchy read error, **data, level 0** — the L1 data cache. MCA bank 1 on Broadwell is the DCU (data cache unit). One instance (Sep 4 21:26) also had the OVER bit set: more errors arrived than the bank could log.

## Why it's not software

| When | Process that happened to be running |
|---|---|
| Aug 31 21:41 | `compile` |
| Sep 3 11:11 | `Finder` (RIP in kernel, APFS in backtrace) |
| Sep 4 21:26 | `mdbulkimport` |
| Sep 4 22:19 | `Dock` |
| Sep 5 00:29 | `Claude` |
| Sep 5 13:19 | `fontd` |

Six different processes, no common denominator. `IA32_MC1_ADDR` is a different physical address every time, so it isn't one stuck cell either. The victim is just whatever thread was on the core when the cache read went bad.

And it's accelerating: Aug 31 → Sep 3 → Sep 4 (×2) → Sep 5 (×2).

## The part that actually matters

The Sep 3 panic faulted with `RIP: 0xffffff800eae3583` — kernel address space — with `com.apple.filesystems.apfs(1934.141.2)` in the backtrace. A machine check inside an APFS code path is a **silent data-corruption risk**. A bad L1D read can hand corrupted bytes to a write without anything downstream noticing.

For the vault, that means: any checksum, `git fsck`, dedup pass, or hash comparison run on this machine from here on is unverified. I'd hold off on the single big rewrite until the data is on different silicon.

## What you can't do about it

L1D is on the CPU die, and RAM on a MacBookPro12,1 is soldered — there's nothing to reseat, no DIMM to swap, no NVRAM/SMC reset that touches this. Apple Diagnostics may or may not flag it; MCEs this intermittent often pass. It's a 2015 board, so repair economics are what they are.

Practical mitigations, in order of how much they'll help:

1. **Get the vault onto another machine or drive.** This is the real answer, and it just moved from "planned" to "urgent."
2. **Reduce sustained load.** Every panic hit during heavy work (Spotlight import, compile, Dropbox). Your load average is **142** three minutes after this boot — Spotlight is reindexing 475 GB again after each crash, which loops you right back into the conditions that trip it. Consider `mdutil -i off /` to break that cycle.
3. **Don't trust Time Machine as the only copy.** Backups written by a CPU that miscomputes are backups of unknown fidelity.
